feedback: If a learner thinks all teeth do the same job or that only the front teeth are used, have them notice which teeth bite versus which chew the apple: incisors cut, molars grind.
Confirm the felt categories: chisel front teeth for cutting, pointed teeth for tearing/gripping, broad back teeth for grinding.
activities.intendedInsight: Even within one mouth, different teeth have different shapes and do different jobs — teeth are not all the same.
learnerActions: Run your tongue over the front, side and back teeth and notice the different shapes before naming them.

Using a mirror, count and locate each tooth type (counts will differ between children at this age because baby teeth are still being replaced and some may be missing): flat chisel-shaped front teeth, pointed teeth beside them, and broad bumpy teeth at the back.
Say aloud which teeth feel sharp/chisel-like and which feel broad, and guess what each shape might be good for.

Bite a firm apple: predict first which teeth you'll use for the first bite and which for chewing, and why; then notice which teeth you actually use — usually the front incisors for the first bite, then the apple is moved to the broad back teeth to grind (a child with missing front teeth may bite with side teeth instead).
activities.title: Feel and map your own teeth

feedback: If a learner says you can't tell diet from teeth, or that all animals have much the same teeth, compare a cat skull and a sheep skull directly: sharp tearing teeth vs broad grinding teeth — tooth shape is a reliable clue to diet.
If a learner reasons from how big or fierce the animal looks, redirect to function: pointed = tear, flat = grind; a large horse has broad flat back teeth for grinding plants despite its size.
Note that plant-eaters are not toothless and meat-eaters are not the only ones with sharp teeth — each diet favours particular tooth proportions.
activities.intendedInsight: Tooth shape is evidence of diet in both directions: you can name a tooth's job, and you can infer an animal's diet from an unfamiliar skull. Large pointed tearing teeth with few broad flat grinding teeth suggest a meat-eater; many broad flat ridged back teeth suggest a plant-eater.
learnerActions: Compare a carnivore, herbivore and omnivore jaw side by side, noticing how tooth proportions differ (large canines and few flat teeth vs broad grinding molars with small or no canines vs a mix of pointed canines and broad flat back teeth).
Play 'whose skull?': match predator and herbivore jaws to diets by their teeth.
Answer: a scientist finds a skull with long pointed teeth at the front and hardly any broad flat teeth at the back — would it eat mostly meat or mostly plants, and what about the teeth tells you?

Discuss: a big grizzly bear and a small pet cat both eat meat and both have sharp canines (the bear also eats lots of plants and has broader back teeth) — is it size that decides tooth shape, or diet? And why would a cow or horse need broad flat teeth at the back?
activities.title: Read a skull's diet from its teeth

feedback: If a learner treats teeth as unrelated to digestion, point out that chewing is the first step that breaks food up before it moves on to the stomach.
Keep tooth-care discussion distinct: it motivates care but does not change the names and jobs of the four tooth types.
activities.intendedInsight: Teeth are not isolated — they are the first mechanical stage of digestion, connecting the teeth topic to the digestive-system topic; tooth care is a real-world application.
learnerActions: Trace the 'mouth' stage of the digestive system, describing teeth as the first, mechanical breakdown of food before it travels on.
Explain how biting, tearing and grinding each prepare food for swallowing.
As an applied extension, discuss why we brush and what causes tooth decay, keeping this separate from naming the tooth types.
activities.title: Teeth as the first step of digestion

feedback: Full understanding: reasons shape→function→diet in both directions — names each job and infers an unfamiliar skull's diet.
Partial understanding: names the tooth types and their jobs but cannot yet confidently infer an unknown animal's diet from its teeth — revisit the skull-comparison activity.
Gap: cannot connect tooth shape to function or diet, or reasons from size/fierceness — return to feeling own teeth and the cat-vs-sheep skull comparison.
activities.intendedInsight: A learner who understands the topic can both name each tooth's job and infer diet from teeth, reasoning from shape to function to diet.
learnerActions: Match each tooth type to its job, and sort teeth into biting / tearing / grinding categories.
Answer a question such as 'which teeth would be especially large and important in a lion's mouth, and why?' giving the shape reason.
Explain in your own words why a herbivore needs broad flat back teeth and a carnivore needs large pointed canines.
activities.title: Consolidate and check understanding
